longQuestions: An operating system (OS) is system software that manages the computer's hardware and software resources, acts as an interface between the user and the hardware, and provides common services to application programs (e.g. Windows, UNIX, Linux, macOS).

Types: (1) Single-user, single-task — one user runs one program at a time (MS-DOS); (2) Single-user, multitasking — one user runs several programs (Windows); (3) Multi-user — many users share the computer at once (UNIX, Linux servers).

(4) Batch processing — similar jobs are collected and executed in batches without user interaction; (5) Time-sharing — the CPU time is divided into slices among many users/programs; (6) Real-time — responds to input within a guaranteed time (air-traffic control, medical devices).

(7) Distributed — manages a group of networked computers as one system; (8) Network OS — provides file/printer sharing and security on a network (Windows Server); (9) Embedded — built into devices such as washing machines, ATMs and mobile phones (Android); (10) Multiprocessing — uses two or more CPUs.
Single-user OS allows only one user to use the computer at a time (MS-DOS, Windows for a personal computer); it needs simple security and resource management.

Multi-user OS allows many users to use the computer resources at the same time through terminals or a network (UNIX, Linux, Windows Server); it must protect each user's data, manage permissions and share CPU, memory and devices fairly.
A process is a program in execution with its own memory space, resources and state; processes are independent and heavyweight, and switching between them is costly.

A thread is the smallest unit of execution within a process (a 'lightweight process'); threads of the same process share its memory and resources, are faster to create and switch, and allow parts of a program to run concurrently.
Multiprogramming keeps several programs in memory and a single CPU switches among them (when one waits for I/O) to keep the CPU busy; programs run concurrently, not truly simultaneously.
Multiprocessing uses two or more CPUs in one computer so that several processes actually execute at the same time; it increases speed and reliability.

A distributed operating system manages a collection of independent computers connected by a network and makes them appear to users as a single system; resources and processing are shared among the machines.

Advantages: resource sharing (files, printers, CPU power); higher speed through parallel processing; reliability — if one machine fails others continue; scalability — computers can be added easily; communication between users.

Disadvantages: complex software and design; security problems because data travels over a network; dependence on the network — failure or slowness affects the whole system; difficult to manage and maintain; higher cost of setup.

Different states of a process: (1) New — the process is being created; (2) Ready — loaded in memory and waiting for the CPU; (3) Running — instructions are being executed by the CPU; (4) Blocked/Waiting — waiting for an event such as I/O completion; (5) Terminated/Exit — finished execution. Transitions: new→ready (admitted), ready→running (dispatched), running→ready (time-out), running→blocked (event wait), blocked→ready (event occurs), running→terminated (exit).

DOS (Disk Operating System), e.g. MS-DOS by Microsoft (1981), is a single-user, single-tasking, command-line operating system. The user types commands (internal like DIR, COPY, DEL, CLS and external like FORMAT, XCOPY) at the prompt (C:\>). It manages files on disks and runs programs one at a time; it has no graphical interface.

Real-time processing systems process data and respond within a strict, guaranteed time limit, so the result is available immediately when needed. Hard real-time systems must never miss deadlines (air-bag control, missile guidance, pacemakers); soft real-time systems tolerate small delays (online booking, video streaming). They are used in industrial control, banking ATMs and flight control.

Embedded operating systems are small, specialised operating systems built into dedicated devices to control their functions; they are fast, reliable and use little memory and power. Examples: the software in washing machines, microwave ovens, cars, digital cameras, ATMs, routers and smart phones (Android, embedded Linux, Windows Embedded).

Functions of an OS: (1) Process management — creating, scheduling and terminating processes; (2) Memory management — allocating and freeing RAM, virtual memory; (3) File management — creating, organising, reading and protecting files and folders.

(4) Device (I/O) management — controlling input/output devices through drivers; (5) Security and protection — passwords, user accounts, access permissions; (6) User interface — command-line or graphical interface.
(7) Resource allocation and error handling; (8) Networking and communication; (9) Booting the computer and loading programs; (10) Monitoring performance and keeping records (accounting).
DOS: single-user, single-tasking, command-line interface, 16-bit, little security, mainly for old personal computers.
Windows: single/multi-user, multitasking, graphical user interface (GUI) with windows, icons and mouse; easy to use; wide software and hardware support; commercial (Microsoft).
UNIX: multi-user, multitasking, very stable and secure; mainly command-line (with optional GUI); portable across hardware; used on servers and workstations; Linux is a free UNIX-like system.
activities: Lab practice — internal DOS commands (built into COMMAND.COM): DIR (list files), CD/MD/RD (change, make, remove directory), COPY, DEL, REN, TYPE, CLS, DATE, TIME, VER. External commands (separate files): FORMAT, XCOPY, CHKDSK, DISKCOPY, TREE, ATTRIB. Students practise each, e.g. MD SCHOOL, CD SCHOOL, COPY CON NOTE.TXT, DIR /P.

Installation steps of Windows (XP/7): set the BIOS to boot from DVD/USB → boot from the setup disk → choose language and keyboard → accept the licence → select 'Custom (new) install' → create/format a partition → files are copied and the computer restarts → enter user name, password and product key → set time zone and network → install drivers. Main features of Windows 7: improved taskbar and jump lists, Aero interface, libraries, better security (UAC), faster performance and HomeGroup networking.

Utility programs (part of the OS) include: Disk Cleanup (removes temporary files), Disk Defragmenter (rearranges file fragments for speed), Backup and Restore, antivirus/Windows Defender, file compression (ZIP), Task Manager and System Restore. Students run each and note its purpose.

Driver installation practice: insert the driver CD or download the driver from the manufacturer's website → open Device Manager → right-click the device (LAN card, sound card, printer, graphics card) → Update/Install driver → browse to the driver file → restart if asked; then test the device. Drivers let the OS communicate with the hardware.
